import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Conjecture 6.39

by B. I. Plotkin

A class of groups $\mathfrak K$ is radical if it is closed under homomorphic images and normal
subgroups, and every group generated by its normal $\mathfrak K$-subgroups belongs to
$\mathfrak K$. The problem asks whether there are first-order axiomatizable radical classes that
are not locally finite and are not the class of all groups. It also asks the concrete variant in
which first-order axiomatizability is replaced by closure under arbitrary Cartesian products and
membership of an infinite cyclic group.

*Reference:* [The Kourovka Notebook](https://arxiv.org/abs/1401.0300v46), Problem 6.39.
-/

namespace Kourovka.«6.39»

/-- A class of groups on small carrier types. The typeclass argument makes membership depend on
the group structure as well as on the carrier type. -/
abbrev GroupClass := (G : Type) → [Group G] → Prop

/-- The function symbols of the first-order language of groups. -/
inductive groupFunc : ℕ → Type
  | mul : groupFunc 2
  | inv : groupFunc 1
  | one : groupFunc 0

/-- The first-order language of groups, with multiplication, inverse, and identity. -/
def groupLanguage : FirstOrder.Language where
  Functions := groupFunc
  Relations := fun _ ↦ Empty

/-- The canonical interpretation of the first-order language of groups on a group. -/
def groupStructure (G : Type) [Group G] : groupLanguage.Structure G where
  funMap := fun {n} f ↦ match n, f with
    | _, .mul => fun x ↦ x 0 * x 1
    | _, .inv => fun x ↦ (x 0)⁻¹
    | _, .one => fun _ ↦ 1
  RelMap := fun {n} r ↦ by
    change Empty at r
    exact r.elim

/-- A group class is isomorphism-closed if isomorphic groups either both belong or both do not
belong to it. -/
def IsIsomorphismClosed (K : GroupClass) : Prop :=
  ∀ (G H : Type) [Group G] [Group H], Nonempty (G ≃* H) → (K G ↔ K H)

/-- A group class is radical if it is isomorphism-closed, is closed under surjective homomorphic
images and normal subgroups, and contains every group generated by its normal members. -/
def IsRadical (K : GroupClass) : Prop :=
  IsIsomorphismClosed K ∧
  (∀ (G H : Type) [Group G] [Group H] (f : G →* H), Function.Surjective f → K G → K H) ∧
  (∀ (G : Type) [Group G] (N : Subgroup G), N.Normal → K G → K N) ∧
  (∀ (G : Type) [Group G],
    (⨆ N : {N : Subgroup G // N.Normal ∧ K N}, (N : Subgroup G)) = ⊤ → K G)

/-- A class of groups is first-order axiomatizable if membership among groups is equivalent to
satisfying some set of sentences in the language of groups. -/
def IsFirstOrderAxiomatizable (K : GroupClass) : Prop :=
  ∃ T : groupLanguage.Theory, ∀ (G : Type) [Group G],
    let _ := groupStructure G
    K G ↔ G ⊨ T

/-- A group is locally finite if every subgroup generated by a finite set is finite. -/
def IsLocallyFiniteGroup (G : Type) [Group G] : Prop :=
  ∀ S : Set G, S.Finite → (Subgroup.closure S : Set G).Finite

/-- A class is closed under arbitrary Cartesian products if the product of every small family of
members is again a member. -/
def IsClosedUnderCartesianProducts (K : GroupClass) : Prop :=
  ∀ (ι : Type) (G : ι → Type) [∀ i, Group (G i)], (∀ i, K (G i)) → K (∀ i, G i)

/--
Do there exist radical classes of groups definable by first-order formulae that are not locally
finite and are different from the class of all groups?

Here “definable by first-order formulae” is read as axiomatizable by a set of sentences in the
first-order language of groups. A class is not locally finite when it contains a group which is
not locally finite.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 3 20]
theorem kourovka.«6.39» : answer(sorry) ↔
    ∃ K : GroupClass,
      IsRadical K ∧ IsFirstOrderAxiomatizable K ∧
      (∃ (G : Type) (_ : Group G), K G ∧ ¬IsLocallyFiniteGroup G) ∧
      (∃ (G : Type) (_ : Group G), ¬K G) := by
  sorry

/--
In particular, does there exist a radical class of groups which is closed under arbitrary
Cartesian products, contains an infinite cyclic group, and is different from the class of all
groups?

The infinite cyclic group is represented by the multiplicative copy of $(\mathbb{Z},+)$. No
first-order definability assumption is imposed in this variant.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 20]
theorem kourovka.«6.39».variants.cartesian_products : answer(sorry) ↔
    ∃ K : GroupClass,
      IsRadical K ∧ IsClosedUnderCartesianProducts K ∧ K (Multiplicative ℤ) ∧
      (∃ (G : Type) (_ : Group G), ¬K G) := by
  sorry

end Kourovka.«6.39»
modeling_decisions: A group class is represented on small carrier types by a predicate depending on both the carrier and its `Group` instance, and is explicitly required to be isomorphism-closed.
Closure under homomorphic images is stated using arbitrary surjective group homomorphisms; closure under normal subgroups uses the induced group structure on a normal `Subgroup`.
A group is generated by its normal class-subgroups when the supremum of all normal subgroups belonging to the class is `⊤`. This is equivalent to being generated by some family of such subgroups.

For the first slot, “definable by formulae of first-order predicate calculus” is read, as directed by the decomposition, as axiomatizable by an arbitrary set of sentences in the first-order language of groups, rather than necessarily by one sentence.
A class is “not locally finite” when it contains a group having a finitely generated infinite subgroup; local finiteness is encoded by finiteness of the closure of every finite set.
Cartesian-product closure quantifies over arbitrary small, possibly empty and infinite, dependent families of groups.
The infinite cyclic group is represented as `Multiplicative ℤ`; isomorphism closure then gives membership of every isomorphic infinite cyclic group.
The second, concrete variant deliberately has no first-order-definability assumption, following its literal wording and the fixed decomposition.

import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Conjecture 6.39

by B. I. Plotkin

A class of groups $\mathfrak{K}$ is said to be *radical* if it is closed under taking
homomorphic images and normal subgroups and if every group generated by its normal
$\mathfrak{K}$-subgroups also belongs to $\mathfrak{K}$. The question proposed relates to
the topic "Radical classes and formulae of Narrow (first order) Predicate Calculus (NPC)".
One can show that the only non-trivial radical class definable by universal formulae of NPC
is the class of all groups. Recently (in a letter to me), G. M. Bergman constructed a family
of locally finite radical classes definable by formulae of NPC. Do there exist similar
classes which are not locally finite and different from the class of all groups? In
particular, does there exist a radical class of groups which is closed under taking
Cartesian products, contains an infinite cyclic group, and is different from the class of
all groups?

Here a class of groups is modelled as a predicate on groups (in a fixed universe), and
"definable by formulae of NPC" is read as: the class is the class of models of some set of
first-order sentences in the language of groups (with function symbols for multiplication,
inversion and the identity).

*Reference:* [The Kourovka Notebook](https://arxiv.org/abs/1401.0300v46)
-/

namespace Kourovka.«6.39»

open FirstOrder FirstOrder.Language

universe u

/-- A class of groups, i.e. a property of groups (in the universe `u`). -/
abbrev GroupClass := (G : Type u) → [Group G] → Prop

/-- A class of groups $\mathfrak{K}$ is *radical* if it is closed under taking homomorphic
images and normal subgroups, and every group generated by its normal
$\mathfrak{K}$-subgroups belongs to $\mathfrak{K}$. -/
structure IsRadicalClass (K : GroupClass.{u}) : Prop where
  /-- $\mathfrak{K}$ is closed under taking homomorphic images. -/
  mem_of_surjective : ∀ {G H : Type u} [Group G] [Group H] (f : G →* H),
    Function.Surjective f → K G → K H
  /-- $\mathfrak{K}$ is closed under taking normal subgroups. -/
  mem_of_normal : ∀ {G : Type u} [Group G] (N : Subgroup G), N.Normal → K G → K N
  /-- A group generated by its normal $\mathfrak{K}$-subgroups belongs to $\mathfrak{K}$. -/
  mem_of_sSup_normal_eq_top : ∀ {G : Type u} [Group G],
    sSup {N : Subgroup G | N.Normal ∧ K N} = ⊤ → K G

/-- A group is *locally finite* if every finitely generated subgroup is finite. -/
def IsLocallyFinite (G : Type u) [Group G] : Prop :=
  ∀ H : Subgroup G, H.FG → Finite H

/-- The function symbols of the first-order language of groups: multiplication (arity `2`),
inversion (arity `1`) and the identity (arity `0`). -/
inductive GroupFunc : ℕ → Type
  | mul : GroupFunc 2
  | inv : GroupFunc 1
  | one : GroupFunc 0

/-- The first-order language of groups: function symbols `*`, `⁻¹`, `1` and no relation
symbols. -/
def groupLanguage : Language where
  Functions := GroupFunc
  Relations _ := Empty

/-- Every group is a structure for the language of groups, interpreting the function symbols
by the group operations. -/
instance instGroupLanguageStructure (G : Type u) [Group G] : groupLanguage.Structure G where
  funMap {n} f := match n, f with
    | _, .mul => fun x => x 0 * x 1
    | _, .inv => fun x => (x 0)⁻¹
    | _, .one => fun _ => 1
  RelMap r _ := Empty.elim r

/-- A class of groups is *definable by formulae of first-order predicate calculus* (i.e. is an
axiomatizable class) if there is a set `T` of first-order sentences in the language of groups
such that a group belongs to the class if and only if it is a model of `T`. -/
def IsAxiomatizable (K : GroupClass.{u}) : Prop :=
  ∃ T : groupLanguage.Theory, ∀ (G : Type u) [Group G], K G ↔ G ⊨ T

/-- The class of all groups is radical. -/
@[category test, AMS 20]
theorem isRadicalClass_top : IsRadicalClass (fun (_ : Type u) _ => True) where
  mem_of_surjective _ _ _ := trivial
  mem_of_normal _ _ _ := trivial
  mem_of_sSup_normal_eq_top _ := trivial

/-- The class of all groups is axiomatizable (by the empty set of sentences). -/
@[category test, AMS 3 20]
theorem isAxiomatizable_top : IsAxiomatizable (fun (_ : Type u) _ => True) :=
  ⟨∅, fun _ _ => ⟨fun _ => inferInstance, fun _ => trivial⟩⟩

/-- The multiplication symbol of the language of groups. -/
abbrev mulFunc : groupLanguage.Functions 2 := GroupFunc.mul

/-- The sentence $\forall x\, y,\ x y = y x$ of the language of groups. -/
def commSentence : groupLanguage.Sentence :=
  ∀' ∀' (mulFunc.apply₂ &0 &1 =' mulFunc.apply₂ &1 &0)

/-- A group satisfies `commSentence` if and only if it is commutative. -/
@[category test, AMS 3 20]
theorem realize_commSentence (G : Type u) [Group G] :
    G ⊨ commSentence ↔ ∀ x y : G, x * y = y * x := by
  simp only [commSentence, Sentence.Realize, Formula.Realize, BoundedFormula.realize_all,
    BoundedFormula.realize_bdEqual]
  rfl

/-- The class of commutative groups is axiomatizable. -/
@[category test, AMS 3 20]
theorem isAxiomatizable_isMulCommutative :
    IsAxiomatizable (fun (G : Type u) _ => IsMulCommutative G) :=
  ⟨{commSentence}, fun G _ => by
    simp only [Theory.model_iff, Set.mem_singleton_iff, forall_eq, realize_commSentence]
    exact ⟨fun h => h.1.1, fun h => ⟨⟨h⟩⟩⟩⟩

/-- A finite group is locally finite. -/
@[category test, AMS 20]
theorem IsLocallyFinite.of_finite (G : Type u) [Group G] [Finite G] : IsLocallyFinite G :=
  fun _ _ => inferInstance

/-- An infinite cyclic group is not locally finite. -/
@[category test, AMS 20]
theorem not_isLocallyFinite_of_isCyclic (G : Type u) [Group G] [IsCyclic G] [Infinite G] :
    ¬ IsLocallyFinite G := by
  intro h
  obtain ⟨g, hg⟩ := IsCyclic.exists_generator (α := G)
  have : (⊤ : Subgroup G).FG :=
    ⟨{g}, by simpa [Subgroup.zpowers_eq_closure] using (Subgroup.eq_top_iff' _).2 hg⟩
  have : Finite G := (Subgroup.topEquiv (G := G)).toEquiv.finite_iff.1 (h ⊤ this)
  exact not_finite G

/--
Do there exist radical classes of groups, definable by formulae of first-order predicate
calculus, which are not locally finite and different from the class of all groups?

A class of groups is *not locally finite* if it contains a group which is not locally finite,
i.e. a group with an infinite finitely generated subgroup. "Definable by formulae of first-order
predicate calculus" is read as: the class is the class of all models of some set of first-order
sentences in the language of groups.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 3 20]
theorem kourovka.«6.39» : answer(sorry) ↔
    ∃ K : GroupClass.{u}, IsRadicalClass K ∧ IsAxiomatizable K ∧
      (∃ (G : Type u) (_ : Group G), K G ∧ ¬ IsLocallyFinite G) ∧
      ∃ (G : Type u) (_ : Group G), ¬ K G := by
  sorry

/--
Does there exist a radical class of groups which is closed under taking Cartesian products,
contains an infinite cyclic group, and is different from the class of all groups?

Here Cartesian products are unrestricted direct products $\prod_{i \in I} G_i$ of arbitrary
(possibly infinite) families of groups.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 20]
theorem kourovka.«6.39».variants.cartesian_products : answer(sorry) ↔
    ∃ K : GroupClass.{u}, IsRadicalClass K ∧
      (∀ (ι : Type u) (G : ι → Type u) [∀ i, Group (G i)],
        (∀ i, K (G i)) → K (∀ i, G i)) ∧
      (∃ (G : Type u) (_ : Group G), IsCyclic G ∧ Infinite G ∧ K G) ∧
      ∃ (G : Type u) (_ : Group G), ¬ K G := by
  sorry

end Kourovka.«6.39»

The table's reading (first slot: axiomatizable radical class containing a non-locally-finite group and ≠ all groups; second slot: radical class closed under Cartesian products containing ℤ and ≠ all groups, without a definability hypothesis) matches the statement. The set-of-sentences vs single-sentence ambiguity the table flags was resolved toward a set of sentences.
modeling_decisions: 'Definable by formulae of NPC' is read as definable by a SET of first-order sentences (axiomatizable/elementary class), following the decomposition notes; the single-sentence (finitely axiomatizable) reading is the stronger special case and is not separately stated.

The language of groups is taken with function symbols (·, ⁻¹, 1) and no relation symbols; since inverse and identity are first-order definable from multiplication in any group, the choice of signature does not affect which classes are axiomatizable.

A class of groups is a predicate on groups in a fixed universe `Type u` (theorems are universe polymorphic). Closure under homomorphic images is stated for all surjective homomorphisms G →* H with H in the same universe; this implies isomorphism-closure, so no separate isomorphism-invariance hypothesis is added.

'Group generated by its normal K-subgroups' is formalized as `sSup {N : Subgroup G | N.Normal ∧ K N} = ⊤`. For the trivial group this hypothesis holds vacuously (sSup ∅ = ⊥ = ⊤), so every radical class contains the trivial group; this agrees with standard radical-class theory and is irrelevant to both questions (which require a non-locally-finite group, resp. an infinite cyclic group, in the class).
'Not locally finite' for a class means the class contains at least one group that is not locally finite (a group with an infinite finitely generated subgroup).
'Different from the class of all groups' is formalized as ∃ G, ¬ K G.
'Closed under Cartesian products' is formalized as closure under unrestricted Pi-products `∀ i, G i` over arbitrary index types ι : Type u (including empty and infinite ι).
'Contains an infinite cyclic group' is formalized as ∃ G, IsCyclic G ∧ Infinite G ∧ K G rather than K (Multiplicative ℤ); these agree because radical classes are isomorphism-closed.
The first slot includes only the radical + first-order-definable hypotheses (no Cartesian-product closure), per the table; the second slot includes no definability hypothesis, per the table.

import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Conjecture 6.39

by B. I. Plotkin

A class of groups $\mathfrak K$ is radical if it is closed under homomorphic images and normal
subgroups, and every group generated by its normal $\mathfrak K$-subgroups is in $\mathfrak K$.
The problem asks whether there is such a first-order axiomatizable class which is not locally
finite and is not the class of all groups. It also asks the particular version in which first-order
axiomatizability is replaced by closure under arbitrary Cartesian products and the class contains
an infinite cyclic group.

*Reference:* [The Kourovka Notebook](https://arxiv.org/abs/1401.0300v46)
-/

namespace Kourovka.«6.39»

open FirstOrder

universe u

/-- The function symbols of the first-order language of groups. -/
inductive GroupFunc : ℕ → Type
  | mul : GroupFunc 2
  | inv : GroupFunc 1
  | one : GroupFunc 0

/-- The first-order language of groups, with multiplication, inversion, and the identity. -/
def groupLanguage : Language where
  Functions := GroupFunc
  Relations := fun _ => Empty

/-- The canonical interpretation of the first-order language of groups on a group. -/
def groupStructure (G : GrpCat.{u}) : groupLanguage.Structure G where
  funMap := fun {n} f =>
    match n, f with
    | _, .mul => fun x => x 0 * x 1
    | _, .inv => fun x => (x 0)⁻¹
    | _, .one => fun _ => 1
  RelMap := fun {_} r => nomatch r

/-- A group is locally finite if each of its finitely generated subgroups is finite. -/
def IsLocallyFinite (G : GrpCat.{u}) : Prop :=
  ∀ H : Subgroup G, H.FG → Finite H

/-- A class of groups is radical if it is invariant under isomorphism, is closed under
homomorphic images and normal subgroups, and contains every group generated by its normal
subgroups which belong to the class. -/
def IsRadical (K : Set GrpCat.{u}) : Prop :=
  (∀ (G H : GrpCat.{u}), Nonempty (G ≃* H) → G ∈ K → H ∈ K) ∧
  (∀ (G H : GrpCat.{u}) (f : G →* H), Function.Surjective f → G ∈ K → H ∈ K) ∧
  (∀ (G : GrpCat.{u}) (H : Subgroup G), H.Normal → G ∈ K → GrpCat.of H ∈ K) ∧
  (∀ G : GrpCat.{u},
    (⨆ (H : Subgroup G) (_ : H.Normal) (_ : GrpCat.of H ∈ K), H) = ⊤ → G ∈ K)

/-- A class of groups is first-order axiomatizable if membership is equivalent to satisfying
some set of first-order sentences in the language of groups. -/
def IsFirstOrderAxiomatizable (K : Set GrpCat.{u}) : Prop :=
  ∃ T : groupLanguage.Theory, ∀ G : GrpCat.{u},
    let _ := groupStructure G
    G ∈ K ↔ G ⊨ T

/-- A class of groups is closed under arbitrary Cartesian products, including products over
infinite or empty index types. -/
def IsClosedUnderCartesianProducts (K : Set GrpCat.{u}) : Prop :=
  ∀ (ι : Type u) (G : ι → GrpCat.{u}),
    (∀ i, G i ∈ K) → GrpCat.of (∀ i, G i) ∈ K

/--
Does there exist a radical class $\mathfrak K$, axiomatizable by a set of first-order sentences
in the language of groups, which contains a group that is not locally finite and differs from the
class of all groups?
-/
@[category research open, AMS 3 20]
theorem kourovka.«6.39» : answer(sorry) ↔
    ∃ K : Set GrpCat.{u}, IsRadical K ∧ IsFirstOrderAxiomatizable K ∧
      (∃ G ∈ K, ¬ IsLocallyFinite G) ∧ K ≠ Set.univ := by
  sorry

/--
In particular, does there exist a radical class $\mathfrak K$ which is closed under arbitrary
Cartesian products, contains the infinite cyclic group $\mathbb Z$, and differs from the class of
all groups? No first-order definability assumption is imposed in this particular question.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 20]
theorem variants.cartesian_products : answer(sorry) ↔
    ∃ K : Set GrpCat.{u}, IsRadical K ∧ IsClosedUnderCartesianProducts K ∧
      GrpCat.of (ULift.{u} (Multiplicative ℤ)) ∈ K ∧ K ≠ Set.univ := by
  sorry

end Kourovka.«6.39»
modeling_decisions: A class of groups is represented as a set of bundled groups `Set GrpCat`, together with explicit isomorphism invariance as required by the decomposition.
The ambiguous phrase “definable by formulae” is modeled as axiomatizability by a set (theory) of first-order sentences; this includes definition by a single sentence as a special case.
“Generated by its normal K-subgroups” is expressed by requiring the join of all normal subgroups whose underlying groups lie in K to be the top subgroup.
“Not locally finite” for a class means that it contains a group having a finitely generated infinite subgroup.
Cartesian-product closure quantifies over arbitrary universe-small index types, including infinite and empty types.

The infinite cyclic group is represented multiplicatively as `ULift (Multiplicative ℤ)` so that it lies in the same carrier universe as the bundled group class; radical-class isomorphism invariance makes the representative immaterial.
No first-order axiomatizability condition is imposed on the Cartesian-products variant, following the literal wording and decomposition notes.
